items.prompt: Define the term ‘monomer’.
items.answer: A monomer is a small, basic molecular unit that can join together with many other identical or similar units to form a larger molecule called a polymer.
items.explanation: Glucose monomers join to form the polysaccharide starch, amino acid monomers join to form proteins, and nucleotide monomers join to form nucleic acids — in each case, many repeating monomers are linked to build a much larger polymer.

items.prompt: Name the TWO types of nucleic acid found in living cells.
items.answer: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid).
items.explanation: Both DNA and RNA are polymers built from repeating nucleotide monomers, but they differ in their sugar component, the number of strands, and which nitrogenous bases they contain.

items.prompt: Describe TWO properties of water that make it essential to living organisms.
items.answer: (1) Water is a good solvent for many substances, due to its polarity, allowing chemical reactions to occur in solution within cells and enabling the transport of dissolved substances around the body. (2) Water has a high specific heat capacity, meaning it can absorb or release large amounts of heat energy while undergoing only a small change in its own temperature, which helps keep the internal temperature of organisms relatively stable.
items.explanation: Both properties arise from the polar nature of the water molecule and the hydrogen bonds this allows between neighbouring water molecules, which together explain why water is so central to metabolism, transport and temperature regulation in living organisms.

items.prompt: Describe the structure of a triglyceride (fat) molecule, referring to glycerol and fatty acids.
items.answer: A triglyceride consists of one glycerol molecule bonded to three fatty acid chains. Each fatty acid is joined to the glycerol by a condensation reaction, forming an ester bond and releasing a water molecule, so that three water molecules are released in total when a full triglyceride is formed.
items.explanation: This condensation-reaction pattern (bonds forming with the release of water) is the same general mechanism used to join monomers together in carbohydrates and proteins, though in a triglyceride only three fatty acid “units” are joined to the central glycerol, rather than a long repeating chain.

items.prompt: Describe the FOUR levels of protein structure: primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary.
items.answer: Primary structure is the specific sequence in which amino acids are joined together in a chain (polypeptide) by peptide bonds. Secondary structure is the local folding of parts of this chain into regular shapes, such as an alpha helix or a beta-pleated sheet, held together by hydrogen bonds. Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the entire polypeptide chain into a specific, stable shape, held together by various bonds and interactions between the amino acid side chains. Quaternary structure occurs only in proteins made of more than one polypeptide chain, and describes how these separate chains are arranged and bonded together to form the final, functional protein.
items.explanation: The precise three-dimensional shape a protein finally folds into (largely determined by its primary sequence) is critical to its function — for example, an enzyme’s tertiary/quaternary shape creates the specific active site needed to bind its substrate.

items.context: A graph shows the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction increasing as temperature rises from 10°C to an optimum at around 37°C, before decreasing sharply as temperature rises further toward 60°C.
items.prompt: Interpret this graph, explaining the effect of temperature on enzyme activity both below and above the optimum temperature.
items.answer: Below the optimum temperature, increasing temperature increases the kinetic energy of both the enzyme and substrate molecules, causing more frequent, higher-energy collisions between them, which increases the rate of the reaction. Above the optimum temperature, the enzyme (a protein) begins to denature — the heat disrupts the bonds holding its tertiary structure in place, permanently changing the shape of its active site so that the substrate can no longer bind effectively, which sharply decreases the reaction rate.
items.explanation: This is why enzyme activity rises then falls with increasing temperature rather than continuing to increase indefinitely: two opposing effects are at work, with increased molecular movement dominating below the optimum, and progressive denaturation dominating above it.

items.context: A learner who has been taught the lock-and-key model reads about the induced-fit model and concludes that the lock-and-key model has been proved wrong and should no longer be taught.
items.prompt: Assess this conclusion. Justify your answer by explaining how the induced-fit model describes the interaction between an enzyme and its substrate.
items.answer: Induced fit refines the lock-and-key model rather than overturning it, and the part the learner was taught first is still doing most of the work. Both models rest on the same central claim: the active site of an enzyme has a shape complementary to its substrate, and it is that complementarity which makes the enzyme specific. A substrate of a different shape cannot bind, so the enzyme cannot catalyse the reaction, which is why sucrase acts on sucrose and not on starch. Where the models differ is in how rigid the fit is. Lock-and-key pictures the active site as a fixed shape into which only the right substrate slots. Induced fit says the active site is flexible: the substrate is not an exact fit at first, and as it enters, the active site changes shape slightly to mould itself around the substrate. That closer contact is what strains the bonds in the substrate and lowers the activation energy, so induced fit explains the catalysis better than a rigid lock can -- a key does not change a lock, but this enzyme does change around its substrate. Specificity survives unchanged, because the active site can only mould itself around a substrate that is already close to complementary. So the honest judgement is that lock-and-key is a useful simplification that gets specificity right and rigidity wrong, and induced fit is the more accurate account. Superseding a model is not the same as disproving it, and teaching the simpler one first is reasonable as long as it is not presented as final.
items.explanation: Level 4 because the learner must judge the relationship between two models -- what the newer one keeps and what it corrects -- rather than choose between them.

items.context: A sample of DNA from one organism is analysed. Adenine makes up 28% of its bases. In a second organism, adenine makes up 31%. In every organism tested, the proportion of adenine matches that of thymine, and the proportion of cytosine matches that of guanine.
items.prompt: Calculate the percentage of guanine in the first organism, showing your working, and explain what this consistent pattern reveals about how the two strands of DNA are held together.
items.answer: If adenine is 28%, then thymine is also 28%, so A and T together account for 56%. The remaining 44% must be cytosine and guanine, and since those two are equal, each is 22%. Guanine is 22%. The pattern holds in every organism because of how the two strands pair. The strands are joined by hydrogen bonds between bases, and the pairing is not random: adenine always bonds with thymine and cytosine always bonds with guanine. This is because a purine, which is a large double-ring base, always pairs with a pyrimidine, which is a small single-ring base, so that every rung of the ladder is the same width and the molecule keeps a constant diameter along its length. The shapes and the positions of the hydrogen-bonding groups allow only these two combinations. Since every adenine on one strand is opposite a thymine on the other, the two must occur in equal numbers in the whole molecule, and the same follows for cytosine and guanine. The proportions differ between organisms because the SEQUENCE differs, but the pairing rule holds regardless, which is why the equalities appear in every organism while the actual percentages do not.
items.explanation: Do the arithmetic in two steps — A equals T, so double it, then split what is left — and the working is the easy part. The reasoning that matters is why the equality is forced: complementary base pairing means each A is physically opposite a T, so the counts cannot differ, and the constant width of the double helix is what requires a large base to pair with a small one.

sections.title: Cells: The Basic Units of Life

items.prompt: Define a ‘cell’.
items.answer: A cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of life, capable of carrying out all the basic life processes needed to sustain life.
items.explanation: Cell theory states that all living organisms are made up of one or more cells, and that all cells arise from pre-existing cells through cell division.

items.prompt: Name TWO structures found in a plant cell that are not found in an animal cell.
items.answer: A cell wall and a chloroplast (a large, permanent central vacuole is also acceptable).
items.explanation: These structures reflect the plant cell’s different requirements: the cell wall provides rigid structural support, the chloroplast enables photosynthesis, and the large central vacuole helps maintain turgor pressure — none of which an animal cell needs in the same way.

items.prompt: Describe the structure and function of the mitochondrion.
items.answer: A mitochondrion has a smooth outer membrane and a folded inner membrane (the folds are called cristae), which encloses a fluid-filled matrix. Mitochondria are the main site of aerobic cellular respiration, breaking down glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy, which is used to produce ATP.
items.explanation: The folded cristae greatly increase the internal surface area of the mitochondrion, providing more space for the enzymes and reactions of aerobic respiration, which is why mitochondria are often described as the “powerhouse” of the cell.

items.prompt: Describe the structure and function of the Golgi apparatus (Golgi body).
items.answer: The Golgi apparatus is a stack of flattened, membrane-bound sacs. It receives proteins and lipids from the endoplasmic reticulum, modifies and packages them into vesicles, and sorts them for transport to their correct destination, either within the cell or for secretion out of the cell.
items.explanation: The Golgi apparatus acts as the cell’s packaging and distribution centre, working closely with the endoplasmic reticulum to ensure that proteins and lipids are correctly processed and sent to where they are needed.

items.context: A learner argues that prokaryotic cells are simply primitive failures, since they lack the organelles that eukaryotic cells have, and that bacteria would be better off if they had them.
items.prompt: Evaluate this argument. Justify your answer by explaining what membrane-bound organelles allow a eukaryotic cell to do.
items.answer: The structural difference is real and "primitive failure" does not follow, because the two cell types succeed by opposite strategies. A eukaryotic cell has a true nucleus enclosing its DNA and a range of membrane-bound organelles -- mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes -- and those membranes divide the cell into separate compartments. That compartmentation is the real advantage: different reactions needing different conditions can run at the same time in the same cell without interfering, respiration proceeding inside mitochondria while digestive enzymes stay safely inside lysosomes where they cannot destroy the cell. A prokaryotic cell has no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles, only ribosomes and a loop of DNA in the cytoplasm, so its reactions share one space and it cannot specialise internally to the same degree. What that buys is speed and economy. A prokaryotic cell is very much smaller, builds and maintains far less structure, and can divide in twenty minutes where a eukaryotic cell takes hours -- so a bacterial population can grow, adapt and spread at a rate no eukaryote matches, which is why bacteria are found in boiling springs, in rock kilometres down and in the human gut in their trillions. Judged by survival and abundance they are the most successful cells on Earth. So the learner has used the eukaryotic cell as the standard and measured everything against it; the correct judgement is that the two are adapted to different ways of living, and organelles are a cost as well as a capability.
items.explanation: The comparison is factually accurate and the ranking is the error. The marks are for naming what compartmentation buys and what it costs.

items.prompt: Explain the process of osmosis, and predict what will happen to an animal cell, such as a red blood cell, if it is placed into a hypotonic solution.
items.answer: Osmosis is the diffusion of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane, from a region of higher water concentration (lower solute concentration) to a region of lower water concentration (higher solute concentration). A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration (and therefore a higher water concentration) than the inside of the red blood cell, so water will move into the cell by osmosis. Because an animal cell has no rigid cell wall to resist this inward movement of water, the cell will swell and may eventually burst (lyse).
items.explanation: This is why intravenous fluids given to patients must be carefully matched in concentration (isotonic) to blood plasma — a hypotonic fluid could cause red blood cells to take up too much water and burst.

items.context: A structure observed under a light microscope has an actual (real) width of 25 μm. In a scientific drawing of the structure, it is drawn with a width of 100 mm. (1 mm = 1 000 μm)
items.prompt: Calculate the magnification of the drawing. Show your working, and give your final answer in the form ‘× ...’.
items.answer: Magnification = × 4 000
items.explanation: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size, using the same units for both. Image size = 100 mm = 100 mm × 1 000 μm/mm = 100 000 μm. Magnification = 100 000 μm ÷ 25 μm = 4 000, so the drawing is magnified × 4 000 relative to the real structure.

items.context: Under a microscope, a student sees two cells. Cell X has a rigid rectangular outline, large clear spaces in its interior, and numerous small green bodies. Cell Y has an irregular rounded outline with no rigid boundary, no green bodies, and no large clear spaces.
items.prompt: Deduce which cell is from a plant and which from an animal, giving THREE structural reasons, and explain how each of those three structures accounts for something the cell can do.
items.answer: Cell X is the plant cell and cell Y the animal cell. Three differences point that way, and each is functional. First, cell X has a rigid rectangular outline, which indicates a cellulose cell wall outside the membrane; the wall resists stretching, so it supports the cell and gives the plant its shape, and it is why plant cells hold a regular geometry while cell Y is rounded and irregular. Second, the numerous small green bodies are chloroplasts, which carry out photosynthesis — so cell X can make its own glucose using light energy, while cell Y, having none, must obtain its food ready-made. Third, the large clear spaces are a large permanent vacuole filled with cell sap; water drawn into it presses the contents against the cell wall, creating the turgor pressure that keeps a non-woody plant upright, and it also stores substances. Cell Y has no such vacuole, or only small temporary ones, because an animal supports itself with a skeleton and muscle instead. Each structure therefore corresponds to a way of life: a plant stays in one place, makes its own food and supports itself by pressure, while an animal moves, eats and supports itself mechanically.
items.explanation: Work from observation to conclusion, and make each structure earn its place by naming what it lets the cell DO — a list of differences answers half the question. The three hang together as one way of life: being fixed in place makes a rigid wall affordable, makes photosynthesis possible, and makes hydraulic support workable, none of which would suit an animal that has to move.

items.prompt: Define mitosis.
items.answer: Mitosis is a type of nuclear division in which one nucleus divides to produce two genetically identical daughter nuclei, each with the same number of chromosomes as the original parent nucleus.
items.explanation: Because the daughter nuclei produced are genetically identical to the parent, mitosis is the type of division used for growth and the repair of damaged tissue, rather than for producing genetically varied sex cells (which instead requires meiosis).

items.prompt: Name the FOUR phases of nuclear division during mitosis, in the correct order.
items.answer: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
items.explanation: These four phases of mitosis are followed by cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm itself, which produces two separate daughter cells once nuclear division is complete.

items.prompt: Describe what happens to the chromosomes during metaphase and during anaphase of mitosis.
items.answer: During metaphase, the chromosomes (each consisting of two sister chromatids) line up individually along the equator (metaphase plate) of the cell, attached to spindle fibres at their centromere. During anaphase, the centromere of each chromosome splits, separating the sister chromatids, which are then pulled to opposite poles of the cell as the spindle fibres shorten.
items.explanation: This precise, spindle-guided separation ensures that each of the two poles of the cell (and therefore each future daughter cell) receives one complete, identical set of chromosomes.

items.prompt: Describe the main events that occur during interphase, before a cell enters mitosis.
items.answer: During interphase, the cell grows in size and carries out its normal metabolic functions, duplicates its organelles, and builds up energy and protein reserves in preparation for division. Critically, the cell also replicates its DNA, so that each chromosome, originally a single strand, becomes duplicated into two identical sister chromatids joined together at a centromere.
items.explanation: Although interphase is sometimes mistakenly thought of as a “resting” stage, it is in fact the longest and most metabolically active part of the cell cycle, during which the essential preparation (especially DNA replication) needed for a successful mitotic division actually takes place.

items.prompt: Name the FOUR phases of mitosis, in the order in which they occur.
items.answer: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
items.explanation: Chromosomes condense and the spindle forms in prophase, chromosomes line up at the equator in metaphase, chromatids are pulled to opposite poles in anaphase, and two new nuclei form in telophase. Interphase, the long growth and DNA-replication stage, comes before all of them and is not part of mitosis.

items.prompt: Explain the biological significance of mitosis for the growth of a multicellular organism and for the repair of damaged tissue.
items.answer: For growth, mitosis increases the total number of cells in the organism’s body, allowing tissues and organs to increase in size as the organism develops from a single fertilised cell into a fully grown, multicellular body. For repair, mitosis allows damaged or dead cells within a tissue to be replaced with new, genetically identical cells, restoring the structure and function of the damaged tissue (for example, replacing skin cells lost through a cut or graze).
items.explanation: In both cases, it is essential that mitosis produces cells that are genetically identical to the original cell, so that the new cells produced are fully capable of carrying out the same specialised function as the surrounding tissue.

items.prompt: Explain why it is important that each daughter cell produced by mitosis receives an identical and complete set of chromosomes.
items.answer: Each chromosome carries specific genetic information needed to produce the proteins a cell requires to carry out its normal structure and function. If a daughter cell received an incomplete set of chromosomes, it would be missing some of this essential genetic information and would be unable to produce all the proteins it needs, likely resulting in the cell malfunctioning or dying; if it received an identical, complete set, it can function normally, in the same way as the parent cell and all other cells produced from it.
items.explanation: This is also why errors in mitosis that result in an incorrect chromosome number in a daughter cell can be so harmful — such cells often function abnormally, and this type of error is associated with some cancers and other developmental problems.

items.prompt: Define ‘meristematic tissue’.
items.answer: Meristematic tissue is plant tissue composed of undifferentiated cells that are able to continue dividing by mitosis throughout the life of the plant.
items.explanation: The cells produced by cell division in meristematic tissue later differentiate into the various types of permanent tissue (such as epidermal, parenchyma, xylem and phloem tissue) found elsewhere in the plant.

items.prompt: Name TWO locations in a plant where apical meristematic tissue is found.
items.answer: At the tip of a root (root apical meristem) and at the tip of a shoot/stem (shoot apical meristem).
items.explanation: Apical meristems are responsible for the plant’s growth in length, extending the root and shoot systems further into the soil and toward the light respectively.

items.prompt: Describe the structure and function of xylem tissue.
items.answer: Xylem tissue is composed mainly of dead, hollow, lignified vessel elements joined end to end to form continuous tubes. It transports water and dissolved mineral ions from the roots to the rest of the plant, while the lignin in its walls also provides structural support to the plant.
items.explanation: Because xylem vessel elements are dead at maturity and lack cell contents or cross-walls, they form an unobstructed, continuous pathway well suited to the rapid, one-way, upward movement of water through the plant.

items.prompt: Describe the structure and function of phloem tissue.
items.answer: Phloem tissue is composed of living sieve tube elements, joined end to end with perforated end walls (sieve plates), together with adjacent companion cells that support them. Phloem transports (translocates) dissolved organic nutrients, mainly sucrose, from the parts of the plant producing or storing them to the parts of the plant using or storing them.
items.explanation: Unlike xylem, phloem sieve tube elements remain living, since active transport processes (supported by their companion cells) are required to load and unload dissolved sugars into and out of the sieve tubes.

items.prompt: Describe the structure and function of the epidermal tissue of a leaf, referring to the cuticle and the stomata.
items.answer: The epidermis is a single layer of tightly packed, transparent cells covering the outer surface of the leaf. Most epidermal cells secrete a waxy, waterproof cuticle over the outer surface, which reduces uncontrolled water loss from the leaf. The epidermis also contains small pores called stomata, each flanked by two guard cells, which can open or close to regulate the exchange of gases (carbon dioxide and oxygen) and the loss of water vapour through transpiration.
items.explanation: The epidermis therefore performs two related protective roles: the cuticle limits water loss over the general leaf surface, while the stomata provide a controllable route for the essential gas exchange needed for photosynthesis, balanced against the risk of excessive water loss.

items.prompt: Name the tissue that transports water in a plant, state the direction in which that water moves, and name the process that drives the movement.
items.answer: Xylem; water moves upward, from root to leaf; the movement is driven by transpiration (the transpiration pull).
items.explanation: Water evaporating from the leaves lowers the pressure at the top of the xylem, and because water molecules cling to one another by cohesion, the whole column is drawn up as one. No energy is spent by the plant, which is how water reaches the top of a very tall tree.

items.prompt: Describe the arrangement of vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) in a typical dicotyledonous root, compared with a typical dicotyledonous stem.
items.answer: In a dicotyledonous root, the xylem forms a central, star- or cross-shaped core at the very centre of the root, with the phloem arranged in separate patches between the arms of the xylem — this central position helps the root resist the pulling (tension) forces exerted on it by the rest of the plant. In a dicotyledonous stem, the vascular tissue is instead arranged in a ring of separate vascular bundles nearer the outer edge of the stem, with the xylem positioned toward the inside of each bundle and the phloem toward the outside — this arrangement provides both flexibility and resistance to the bending forces a stem experiences.
items.explanation: This difference in arrangement reflects the different mechanical stresses each organ must withstand: a root is mainly subjected to pulling/tension forces, favouring a strong central xylem core, while a stem must resist bending, favoring a ring of vascular bundles nearer its outer circumference.

items.context: A learner suggests that a leaf would work better if its stomata were on the upper surface, since that is the side facing the sun and the light is strongest there.
items.prompt: Evaluate this suggestion. Justify your answer by referring to how the position of each leaf layer suits its function.
items.answer: The suggestion attaches the stomata to the wrong requirement: they are pores for gas exchange, and light does not enter through them. A leaf is layered so that each tissue sits where its job is done. The upper epidermis is transparent and covered by a waxy cuticle, so light passes through it while water loss is reduced. Directly beneath it is the palisade mesophyll -- long cells packed closely in columns, densely filled with chloroplasts -- placed there because it is nearest the light and absorbs most of it. Below that is the spongy mesophyll, loosely arranged with large air spaces between the cells, which lets carbon dioxide diffuse freely to every photosynthesising cell and lets oxygen diffuse out. The stomata are in the lower epidermis, opening into those air spaces, so the gases have a direct route in and out. Light never needs to pass through a stoma, so putting them on top would gain the leaf nothing. It would cost a great deal. The upper surface faces the sun and is the hotter and drier of the two, so stomata there would lose water vapour far faster, and rain and dust would block them. The lower surface is shaded by the leaf itself, cooler, and the air just beneath it is more humid, which reduces the concentration gradient driving water vapour out. So the arrangement lets the leaf take in carbon dioxide while losing as little water as possible, and the learner has optimised for the one requirement the stomata do not serve.
items.explanation: Level 4 because the suggestion is sensible if stomata admit light, and the judgement requires knowing what each layer is positioned for.

items.prompt: Explain why parenchyma is described as a relatively unspecialised plant tissue, and describe TWO different functions it performs in different parts of a plant.
items.answer: Parenchyma is described as relatively unspecialised because its cells are living, have thin cell walls, and retain the ability to divide and differentiate into other cell types if needed, unlike more specialised tissues such as xylem or phloem, which are permanently committed to one specific structure and function. Functions: (1) In the mesophyll of a leaf, parenchyma cells contain chloroplasts and carry out photosynthesis. (2) In organs such as roots, stems and fruits, parenchyma cells are used to store substances such as starch and water.
items.explanation: Because parenchyma cells are not permanently locked into one highly specialised structure, this same basic tissue type is able to take on very different roles — photosynthesis in a green leaf, or storage in a fleshy root or fruit — depending on where in the plant it is located.

items.prompt: Define a ‘tissue’.
items.answer: A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to perform a specific function.
items.explanation: Different tissue types combine to form organs (such as the heart or stomach), and different organs work together as organ systems (such as the circulatory system) to carry out the major life functions of the body.

items.prompt: Name the FOUR main types of animal tissue.
items.answer: Epithelial tissue, connective tissue, muscle tissue and nervous tissue.
items.explanation: Every organ in the body is built from a combination of these four basic tissue types, arranged and specialised in different ways to carry out the organ’s particular function.

items.prompt: Describe the general structure of epithelial tissue, and state its main functions.
items.answer: Epithelial tissue is composed of cells that are tightly packed together, with very little material between them, forming continuous sheets of cells. It covers external body surfaces and lines internal cavities and organs, such as the skin surface and the lining of the gut, and its main functions include protection, secretion and absorption, depending on its location.
items.explanation: The tight packing of epithelial cells makes this tissue especially well suited to forming an effective protective or selectively permeable boundary, whether on the outside of the body or lining an internal organ.

items.prompt: Describe the structure and function of cardiac muscle tissue.
items.answer: Cardiac muscle tissue is composed of branched, striated (banded) muscle cells, joined end to end at specialised junctions called intercalated discs, with each cell typically containing a single nucleus. It contracts rhythmically and involuntarily throughout an organism’s life, without fatiguing, in order to pump blood through the heart.
items.explanation: The intercalated discs allow electrical signals to pass rapidly between adjacent cardiac muscle cells, helping the heart’s chambers contract in a coordinated, wave-like manner rather than as separate, unsynchronised cells.

items.context: Two muscle samples. Sample P is made of very long cells with many nuclei and clear stripes across them; it contracts powerfully and quickly but tires within minutes. Sample Q is made of short spindle-shaped cells with one nucleus each and no stripes; it contracts slowly and can stay contracted for hours without tiring.
items.prompt: Identify each type of muscle, giving a structural reason, and explain how the properties of each suit the job it does in the body.
items.answer: Sample P is skeletal muscle: long multinucleated cells with visible striations are characteristic of it. Sample Q is smooth muscle: short spindle-shaped cells with a single nucleus and no striations. The properties match the work each does. Skeletal muscle moves the skeleton, and that work is powerful, fast and intermittent — running, lifting, throwing — so the muscle is built for force and speed and is under voluntary control, since these movements have to be chosen. Tiring is acceptable because such efforts are short and are followed by rest. Smooth muscle is found in the walls of hollow organs and blood vessels, where the work is slow and sustained: moving food along the gut by peristalsis, holding a blood vessel partly narrowed for hours, keeping the bladder wall under tension. Fatiguing would be disastrous there, since these activities never stop, so smooth muscle is built for endurance rather than power and works involuntarily, without conscious attention. Each type therefore trades what it does not need for what it does: skeletal muscle trades endurance for power, smooth muscle trades power for the ability to keep going.
items.explanation: Identify from the structural clues — striations and many nuclei against spindle shape and one nucleus — then let the properties explain the placement. The trade-off is the useful idea: no muscle is both powerful and tireless, so where each type is found in the body tells you which half of that bargain its job requires.

items.prompt: Name the THREE main parts of a neuron.
items.answer: The cell body, the dendrites and the axon.
items.explanation: The cell body holds the nucleus and does the cell's housekeeping; the dendrites are short branches that receive impulses from other neurons; and the axon is the single long fibre that carries the impulse away, often wrapped in a fatty myelin sheath that speeds transmission.

items.prompt: Describe the structure of a neuron (nerve cell), referring to the cell body, dendrites and axon, and explain how this structure suits it to its function.
items.answer: A neuron has a cell body, containing the nucleus and most of the cell’s organelles; short, branched extensions called dendrites, which receive nerve impulses from other neurons and carry them toward the cell body; and a single, typically much longer extension called the axon, which carries nerve impulses away from the cell body toward the next neuron or an effector (such as a muscle). This structure suits the neuron to rapid, directional transmission of nerve impulses — the many branching dendrites allow it to receive signals from numerous other neurons, while the long axon allows a single impulse to be carried quickly over a considerable distance to a specific, precise destination.
items.explanation: Some axons are additionally insulated by a fatty myelin sheath, which further increases the speed at which nerve impulses can travel along the axon, allowing very rapid communication across the nervous system.

items.prompt: Explain how connective tissue differs from epithelial tissue in terms of the arrangement of its cells and the presence of a matrix, and give ONE example of a connective tissue.
items.answer: In epithelial tissue, cells are packed tightly together with very little material between them, forming continuous sheets. In connective tissue, the cells are typically widely spaced from one another, embedded within a substantial non-living extracellular matrix, which can be fluid (as in blood), jelly-like, or solid and rigid (as in bone or cartilage), depending on the specific type of connective tissue. Example: bone (cartilage, tendon, ligament, blood and adipose/fat tissue are also acceptable).
items.explanation: This difference in matrix amount and composition explains the very different physical properties of connective tissues compared with epithelial tissue — for example, the mineral-rich, solid matrix of bone gives it great rigidity and strength, a property epithelial tissue (with almost no matrix of its own) does not share.

items.context: A learner argues that since cardiac muscle never fatigues, a heart attack cannot be caused by the heart muscle failing, and must be a problem with the nerves controlling it.
items.prompt: Assess this argument. Justify your answer by explaining why cardiac muscle does not fatigue.
items.answer: The premise is true and the conclusion is wrong, because cardiac muscle does not fatigue for a reason that a heart attack removes. Cardiac muscle resists fatigue by a combination of features. Its cells are packed with mitochondria and richly supplied with blood through the coronary arteries, so oxygen and glucose arrive continuously and it respires aerobically essentially all the time, which means lactic acid does not accumulate as it does in skeletal muscle pushed beyond its oxygen supply. Its cells are branched and joined by intercalated discs, so the contraction spreads as a co-ordinated wave, and it is myogenic -- it generates its own rhythm and has a brief rest between beats built into every cycle. The crucial point is the first: freedom from fatigue depends absolutely on that continuous oxygen supply. A heart attack is what happens when a coronary artery is blocked, so the supply to part of the heart muscle stops. Those cells cannot respire aerobically, and cardiac muscle is not built to work anaerobically for long, so they are damaged within minutes and die. The failure is therefore precisely a failure of the heart muscle, caused by the loss of the condition that made it tireless -- not a nerve problem. The learner's argument also assumes the beat depends on nerves, and it does not: the heart generates its own beat and nerves only modify the rate.
items.explanation: A true premise used to exclude the actual cause. The marks are for seeing that the resistance to fatigue is conditional on the blood supply.

items.prompt: Define photosynthesis.
items.answer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants (and some other organisms) use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
items.explanation: Photosynthesis is the primary process by which energy from sunlight enters most food chains, ultimately supporting almost all other forms of life on Earth.

items.prompt: Name the organelle in which photosynthesis takes place.
items.answer: The chloroplast.
items.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, the green pigment that absorbs light energy needed to drive photosynthesis, and are found mainly in the mesophyll cells of a leaf.

items.prompt: Describe the structure of a chloroplast, referring to the grana, thylakoids and stroma.
items.answer: A chloroplast has an outer double membrane enclosing a fluid-filled matrix called the stroma. Within the stroma are stacks of flattened, membrane-bound sacs called thylakoids; a stack of thylakoids is called a granum (plural grana). Chlorophyll is embedded in the thylakoid membranes.
items.explanation: This internal structure separates the two main stages of photosynthesis: the light-dependent reactions occur on/in the thylakoid membranes (where chlorophyll is located), while the light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) occur in the surrounding stroma.

items.prompt: Describe what happens during the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.
items.answer: Chlorophyll in the thylakoid membranes absorbs light energy, which is used to split (photolyse) water molecules into oxygen, hydrogen ions and electrons — the oxygen is released as a by-product. The captured light energy is also used to produce ATP (from ADP and phosphate) and to combine hydrogen ions and electrons with NADP to form NADPH, both of which are then used to power the light-independent reactions.
items.explanation: The light-dependent reactions convert light energy into chemical energy (stored in ATP and NADPH) and produce oxygen as a by-product of splitting water — this is the only stage of photosynthesis that directly requires light.

items.prompt: Describe what happens during the light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) of photosynthesis.
items.answer: Carbon dioxide from the air is "fixed" (combined) with an existing 5-carbon molecule already present in the stroma, in a reaction catalysed by an enzyme. Using the ATP and NADPH produced during the light-dependent reactions, this combined molecule is then converted through a series of steps into glucose, while also regenerating the original 5-carbon molecule so the cycle can continue.
items.explanation: Although the light-independent reactions do not directly require light, they depend entirely on the ATP and NADPH supplied by the light-dependent reactions, so photosynthesis as a whole still stops in the absence of light once existing ATP/NADPH stores are used up.

items.context: A graph shows the rate of photosynthesis increasing steadily as light intensity increases, before levelling off at a constant maximum rate despite further increases in light intensity.
items.prompt: Interpret this graph, explaining why the rate of photosynthesis eventually stops increasing even as light intensity continues to rise.
items.answer: At low light intensities, light is the limiting factor — increasing light intensity directly increases the rate of the light-dependent reactions, and hence the overall rate of photosynthesis. Once the graph levels off, light is no longer the limiting factor; instead, some other factor (such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature) has now become limiting, meaning the rate of photosynthesis cannot increase further no matter how much more light is provided, until that new limiting factor is itself increased.
items.explanation: This illustrates the general principle of limiting factors: the rate of a process that depends on multiple factors is always constrained by whichever factor is currently in shortest supply relative to what is needed, and increasing any other factor beyond that point has no further effect until the actual limiting factor is addressed.

items.prompt: Explain why increasing the carbon dioxide concentration around a plant increases its rate of photosynthesis, up to a certain point.
items.answer: Carbon dioxide is a required reactant for the light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle), where it is fixed and eventually converted into glucose. Increasing the concentration of carbon dioxide available to the plant increases the rate at which this fixation step can occur, increasing the overall rate of photosynthesis — but only up to the point where some other factor (such as light intensity or temperature) becomes the new limiting factor, beyond which further increases in carbon dioxide have no additional effect.
items.explanation: This is why carbon dioxide enrichment is sometimes used in greenhouses to increase crop growth rates, but only provides a benefit up to the point where another factor (typically light or temperature) becomes limiting instead.

items.prompt: Describe TWO structural adaptations of a leaf that make it well suited for photosynthesis.
items.answer: (1) The leaf has a large, flat surface area, which maximises the amount of sunlight it can absorb. (2) The upper mesophyll layer (the palisade layer) contains cells packed closely together and oriented vertically, each containing many chloroplasts, maximising light absorption near the upper (light-facing) surface of the leaf.
items.explanation: Both adaptations directly increase the amount of light energy the leaf can capture: a larger surface area intercepts more incoming sunlight overall, while densely packed, chloroplast-rich palisade cells near the surface make efficient use of the light that is captured.

items.prompt: Define ingestion.
items.answer: Ingestion is the process of taking food into the body through the mouth.
items.explanation: Ingestion is the first stage of the overall process of nutrition, occurring before digestion (the physical and chemical breakdown of food) and absorption (the uptake of digested nutrients into the blood).

items.prompt: Name the enzyme found in saliva that begins the digestion of starch in the mouth.
items.answer: Salivary amylase.
items.explanation: Salivary amylase breaks down starch into shorter chains of sugar (maltose), beginning the chemical digestion of carbohydrates even before food reaches the stomach.

items.prompt: Describe the role of the stomach in digestion.
items.answer: The stomach churns food through muscular contractions (mechanical digestion), mixing it with gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid (which kills many bacteria and provides the acidic environment needed for stomach enzymes to work) and the enzyme pepsin (which begins the chemical digestion of proteins).
items.explanation: The stomach performs both mechanical digestion (physically breaking down food into smaller pieces through churning) and chemical digestion (using acid and pepsin to begin breaking down protein molecules), producing a semi-liquid mixture called chyme that is gradually released into the small intestine.

items.prompt: Describe the role of the small intestine in digestion and absorption.
items.answer: The small intestine completes the chemical digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats, using enzymes it produces itself along with enzymes and bile delivered from the pancreas and liver/gall bladder. Its inner lining is covered in millions of small, finger-like projections called villi (each covered in even smaller microvilli), which greatly increase the surface area available for the absorption of digested nutrients (such as glucose and amino acids) into the bloodstream.
items.explanation: The small intestine is the primary site of both the completion of digestion and the absorption of nutrients, with its highly folded, villus-covered lining specifically adapted to maximise the surface area available for efficient nutrient uptake.

items.prompt: Describe the role of bile in the digestion of fats.
items.answer: Bile, produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder, is released into the small intestine, where it emulsifies fats — breaking large fat droplets into many smaller droplets, which greatly increases the total surface area of fat exposed to the digestive enzyme lipase.
items.explanation: Bile itself does not chemically digest fat (it contains no digestive enzyme); its role is purely physical (emulsification), which makes the subsequent chemical digestion of fat by lipase far more efficient than it would be on large, undivided fat droplets.

items.context: A single villus is about 1 mm long, is covered in a layer one cell thick, and contains a dense network of blood capillaries together with a single lacteal. Blood flows through the capillaries continuously.
items.prompt: Explain how the thin covering and the continuous blood flow each contribute to fast absorption, and explain why a villus needs a lacteal as well as capillaries.
items.answer: The covering being one cell thick means a digested nutrient has only a very short distance to travel between the gut contents and the blood. Rate of diffusion falls as distance rises, so minimising the barrier maximises the rate at which glucose and amino acids cross. The continuous blood flow does something different: it carries absorbed nutrients away as fast as they arrive, so their concentration in the capillary is kept low. That maintains a steep concentration gradient between the gut contents and the blood, and the gradient is what drives the absorption. Without the flow, the capillary would quickly reach the same concentration as the gut and absorption would stop, however thin the barrier was. The lacteal is needed because the products of fat digestion are not handled the same way. Fatty acids and glycerol are reassembled into fats inside the villus cells and packaged into droplets that are too large to pass into a blood capillary. The lacteal is a lymph vessel, with larger gaps in its wall, so these droplets can enter it instead. They travel in the lymph and are emptied into the bloodstream later, near the heart — which is why fats bypass the liver on their first pass while sugars and amino acids do not.
items.explanation: The two features solve different halves of the same problem: the thin wall shortens the DISTANCE, the blood flow maintains the GRADIENT, and either alone would leave absorption slow. The lacteal is the part most often left out, and the reason it exists is a matter of particle size — fat is repackaged into droplets too big for a capillary, so it needs a vessel with a leakier wall.

items.prompt: Describe the role of the pancreas in digestion, referring to the different types of digestive enzymes it produces.
items.answer: The pancreas produces and releases a mixture of digestive enzymes into the small intestine (via the pancreatic duct), including pancreatic amylase (continuing the digestion of any remaining starch into simple sugars), pancreatic protease (continuing the digestion of proteins into amino acids), and pancreatic lipase (digesting emulsified fats into fatty acids and glycerol). The pancreas also releases sodium hydrogen carbonate, which neutralises the acidic chyme arriving from the stomach, providing the more alkaline conditions these pancreatic enzymes require to function effectively.
items.explanation: Because the pancreas supplies enzymes capable of digesting all three major classes of food molecules (carbohydrates, proteins and fats) into the small intestine, it plays a central role in completing chemical digestion, working alongside the small intestine’s own enzymes and the bile supplied by the liver.

items.context: A patient taking a painkiller that suppresses the stomach's protective mucus develops an ulcer. They ask whether taking the tablet on a full stomach, so that food "soaks up" the acid, would prevent it.
items.prompt: Assess the patient's proposal. Justify your answer by explaining how the stomach lining is normally protected.
items.answer: The suggestion helps a little and does not address the cause. The stomach secretes hydrochloric acid and pepsin, which digest protein -- and the stomach wall is itself made of protein, so it needs active protection. That protection is a thick layer of alkaline mucus secreted onto the lining, continuously replaced, which keeps the acid and pepsin away from the cells beneath, together with a rapid turnover of the lining cells themselves. This drug suppresses the production of that mucus. So the ulcer is not caused by more acid but by less defence: a normal amount of acid now reaches an unprotected wall and digests it. Food does buffer the stomach contents and raise the pH somewhat while it is present, which is why taking the tablet with a meal genuinely reduces irritation and is standard advice. But the effect lasts only as long as the meal does, the stomach responds to food by secreting more acid, and none of it restores the mucus barrier -- so the wall stays unprotected for most of the day. The measures that address the mechanism are a drug that reduces acid secretion taken alongside, or a different painkiller that does not suppress the mucus, and the patient should raise it with their doctor rather than rely on timing meals.
items.explanation: The suggestion is reasonable and partly effective, so the marks are for distinguishing what reduces a symptom from what removes the cause.

items.prompt: Define cellular respiration.
items.answer: Cellular respiration is the process by which cells break down glucose (or other organic molecules) to release energy, which is used to produce ATP.
items.explanation: Cellular respiration occurs continuously in living cells, providing the ATP needed to power essentially all cellular processes, from muscle contraction to active transport.

items.prompt: Name the organelle in which most of the reactions of aerobic respiration take place.
items.answer: The mitochondrion.
items.explanation: Mitochondria are often described as the "powerhouse" of the cell, since they are the main site where glucose is fully broken down using oxygen to produce large amounts of ATP.

items.prompt: Write the overall word equation for aerobic cellular respiration.
items.answer: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy, released as ATP)
items.explanation: Aerobic respiration fully breaks down glucose in the presence of oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide and water as waste products, along with a large amount of usable energy captured in ATP.

items.context: Yeast is grown in sugar solution in two sealed flasks. Flask 1 is bubbled with air throughout; Flask 2 has all air excluded. After 24 hours, Flask 1 contains far more yeast cells and no alcohol. Flask 2 contains fewer cells and a measurable concentration of alcohol. Both flasks started with the same amount of sugar, and both have used it all.
items.prompt: Explain why the same amount of sugar produced so many more cells in Flask 1, and explain what the alcohol in Flask 2 tells you about how completely the sugar was broken down.
items.answer: Both flasks respire the same sugar, but they release very different amounts of energy from it. With oxygen present, Flask 1 respires aerobically: glucose is broken down completely to carbon dioxide and water, releasing a large quantity of ATP per glucose molecule. Growth and cell division cost energy, so more ATP means more new cells, which is why the same sugar supported far more yeast. Without oxygen, Flask 2 must ferment: glucose is broken down only to ethanol and carbon dioxide, releasing very little ATP per glucose molecule, so the same sugar funded far fewer divisions. The alcohol is the evidence of that incompleteness. Ethanol is still an energy-containing organic molecule — it burns — so the fact that it is left over shows the yeast could not extract all the energy from the glucose and abandoned the breakdown partway. Aerobic respiration leaves carbon dioxide and water, neither of which holds usable energy, which is the sign that the molecule was taken all the way. So the waste product itself tells you how far the process went.
items.explanation: Trace the energy rather than the gas: the difference in cell numbers is a measure of ATP yield, since growth is what the yeast spends ATP on. The strongest move in the second half is recognising that ETHANOL STILL CONTAINS ENERGY — a fuel as a waste product is direct evidence of incomplete breakdown, and it is also, incidentally, why brewing works at all.

items.context: An athlete runs a 400 m race in under a minute and finishes barely able to stand, with burning legs. Another athlete runs a marathon for over three hours and finishes tired but able to keep moving. Both were respiring throughout.
items.prompt: Explain why a race lasting under a minute leaves the muscles in a worse state than one lasting three hours, referring to the type of respiration each athlete relied on.
items.answer: The difference is whether the oxygen supply could keep up with the demand. The marathon runner works below the rate at which their heart and lungs can deliver oxygen, so the muscles respire aerobically throughout: glucose is broken down completely, the waste products are carbon dioxide and water, both of which are removed easily, and nothing accumulates. The pace is sustainable precisely because it is matched to oxygen delivery, which is why three hours is possible. The 400 m runner works far above that rate. Oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough, so the muscles supplement aerobic respiration with anaerobic respiration, which yields far less ATP per glucose and produces lactic acid. The lactic acid accumulates in the muscle tissue, lowering its pH, which interferes with the enzymes and the contraction mechanism and causes the burning sensation and the loss of power. So the shorter race is more damaging because its intensity forces a pathway that leaves a harmful product behind, while the longer one, though far greater in total work, never exceeds the oxygen supply and leaves nothing to clear up.
items.explanation: The comparison turns on RATE rather than total effort, which is the point most easily missed: the marathon involves vastly more work overall and still leaves the muscles in better condition, because the work was done within the oxygen supply. It is also worth noticing that anaerobic respiration is not a failure but a stopgap — it buys power the oxygen supply cannot fund, at the cost of a product that then has to be dealt with.

items.prompt: Explain why anaerobic respiration releases far less ATP per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration.
items.answer: Anaerobic respiration only partially breaks down the glucose molecule (for example, converting it only as far as lactic acid), whereas aerobic respiration fully breaks glucose down all the way into carbon dioxide and water. Because the lactic acid produced by anaerobic respiration still contains most of the chemical energy that was originally present in the glucose molecule, only a small proportion of that total available energy is actually released and captured as ATP during anaerobic respiration.
items.explanation: This is why an organism relying only on anaerobic respiration must break down considerably more glucose to obtain the same total amount of ATP that a smaller amount of glucose would provide via aerobic respiration.

items.prompt: Define gaseous exchange.
items.answer: Gaseous exchange is the diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide between an organism and its environment (or, internally, between the air in the lungs and the blood).
items.explanation: In humans, gaseous exchange occurs mainly in the lungs, where oxygen diffuses from inhaled air into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the air to be exhaled.

items.prompt: Name the tiny air sacs in the lungs where gaseous exchange takes place.
items.answer: Alveoli (singular: alveolus).
items.explanation: The lungs contain hundreds of millions of alveoli, providing an enormous total surface area for gaseous exchange between the air and the surrounding blood capillaries.

items.prompt: Describe the structure of the trachea, and explain the function of the C-shaped rings of cartilage found along its length.
items.answer: The trachea is a tube lined with ciliated epithelial cells and mucus-secreting goblet cells, reinforced along its length by a series of C-shaped rings of cartilage. These cartilage rings keep the trachea permanently open (preventing it from collapsing), while the gap in each "C" (facing the oesophagus) allows the oesophagus to expand slightly during swallowing.
items.explanation: Without this cartilage support, the trachea (a soft-walled tube) would be at risk of collapsing under the pressure changes involved in breathing, which would obstruct the essential airflow to and from the lungs.

items.prompt: Describe the mechanism of inhalation (breathing in).
items.answer: The diaphragm (a dome-shaped muscle beneath the lungs) contracts and flattens, while the external intercostal muscles between the ribs contract, pulling the rib cage upward and outward. Together, these movements increase the volume of the thoracic (chest) cavity, which decreases the air pressure inside the lungs relative to the air pressure outside the body. Because air flows from a region of higher pressure to lower pressure, air is drawn into the lungs through the airways.
items.explanation: This mechanism works entirely on the basis of a pressure difference created by increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity — air does not need to be actively "pulled" in by any other means, since it naturally flows down the pressure gradient created by this volume change.

items.prompt: Describe THREE structural features of the alveoli that adapt them for efficient gaseous exchange.
items.answer: (1) Alveoli have very thin walls (a single layer of flattened epithelial cells), minimising the distance over which gases must diffuse. (2) Alveoli are surrounded by a dense network of blood capillaries, also with thin walls, maintaining a strong diffusion gradient by continuously carrying oxygen away and carbon dioxide toward the alveoli. (3) The huge number of alveoli in the lungs provides an enormous total surface area for gaseous exchange to occur across.
items.explanation: These same three general features — a short diffusion distance, a well-maintained concentration gradient, and a large surface area — are the hallmark adaptations of essentially every efficient exchange surface found in living organisms.

items.context: Emphysema destroys the walls between neighbouring alveoli, so that many small air sacs merge into fewer, much larger ones. A healthy pair of lungs presents a gas-exchange surface of about 70 m². In advanced emphysema this can fall to about 30 m². The total volume of air the lungs hold is not reduced, and may increase.
items.prompt: Explain why merging small alveoli into larger ones reduces the surface area even though the volume is unchanged, and explain why a person with emphysema becomes breathless despite having plenty of air in their lungs.
items.answer: Surface area and volume do not scale together. Dividing a given volume into many small compartments produces far more total surface than leaving it as a few large ones, because each small sac contributes its own wall — this is why the lungs are built as millions of tiny alveoli rather than as two bags. Merging them destroys walls without removing air, so the volume stays the same or rises while the surface falls, in this case from about 70 m² to about 30 m². The breathlessness follows because gas exchange depends on surface area, not on how much air is present. Oxygen can only enter the blood where air meets an alveolar wall with a capillary on the other side, and less than half that surface now remains, so oxygen enters the blood too slowly to meet the body’s demand. The patient breathes harder in an attempt to compensate, and feels breathless, but moving more air through the lungs cannot make up for having too little surface for it to cross. That is also why the air trapped in the enlarged sacs is of little use: air in the middle of a large sac is nowhere near a wall it can diffuse across.
items.explanation: The surface-to-volume relationship is the whole of the first half, and it is the same reason alveoli, villi and root hairs are all small and numerous. The second half corrects the intuitive but wrong idea that breathlessness means not enough air: the limiting factor is the AREA available for crossing, which is why a patient can have over-inflated lungs and still be short of oxygen.

items.context: A smoker of thirty years says there is no point stopping now, since the damage to their airways is already done.
items.prompt: Evaluate this reasoning, referring to the effect of smoking on the cilia lining the airways.
items.answer: Some of the damage is permanent and a great deal of it is not, so the conclusion does not follow. Smoke paralyses and then destroys the cilia -- the tiny hair-like projections that sweep a film of mucus, with trapped dust and bacteria, up and out of the airways. Without them, mucus and everything caught in it collects in the lungs, which is why smokers cough persistently and are more prone to chest infections. Smoke also irritates the lining into producing more mucus, so there is more to clear and less means of clearing it, and over years it damages the alveolar walls, producing emphysema. The emphysema is irreversible: alveolar walls do not grow back. But the cilia are not in that category. Ciliary function begins to recover within days to months of stopping, so mucus clearance improves, the cough eases and the rate of chest infections falls. Lung function continues to decline with age in everyone, and stopping returns the smoker to roughly the normal rate of decline rather than the accelerated one, so every remaining year is better than it would have been. Risk of lung cancer also falls steadily with years since quitting. So the smoker is right that they cannot undo the emphysema and wrong that this makes stopping pointless -- what is recoverable is recovered, and what is not stops getting worse.
items.explanation: The premise is partly true, which is what makes it persuasive. The judgement requires separating the reversible damage from the irreversible.

items.context: A patient with emphysema is breathless. A relative points out that a lung function test shows the patient's lungs hold MORE air than normal, and argues that the breathlessness therefore cannot be a lung problem.
items.prompt: Assess the relative's argument. Justify your answer by referring to what determines the rate of gaseous exchange.
items.answer: The measurement is correct and the inference from it is wrong, because volume is not what gaseous exchange depends on. In emphysema the walls between adjacent alveoli break down, so many small air sacs merge into fewer, larger ones. That does increase the volume of air the lungs hold, and it also makes the lungs less elastic so air is trapped, which is why the test reads high. But exchange happens across the alveolar surface, and its rate depends on the total surface area available, on the thinness of the barrier and on the concentration gradient. A given volume divided into very many small sacs presents an enormous surface; the same volume as a few large ones presents far less. So merging alveoli destroys surface area while increasing volume -- the two move in opposite directions, which is exactly what the relative has not allowed for. Less surface means less oxygen diffuses into the blood per breath, the patient breathes harder to compensate, and the trapped air makes each breath mechanically harder as well. The breathlessness is therefore a lung problem, and the high reading is one of its signs rather than evidence against it.
items.explanation: A real measurement pointing the wrong way. The marks are for knowing that exchange scales with surface, not volume.

items.prompt: Define excretion.
items.answer: Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste products (substances produced by the body’s own chemical reactions) from the body.
items.explanation: Excretion is distinct from egestion (the removal of undigested food/faeces, which was never actually absorbed into the body’s cells), since excreted substances are true metabolic waste products.

items.prompt: Name the functional and structural unit of the kidney responsible for producing urine.
items.answer: The nephron.
items.explanation: Each kidney contains roughly a million nephrons, each independently carrying out the processes of filtration, reabsorption and secretion that together produce urine.

items.prompt: Describe the process of ultrafiltration that occurs in the glomerulus and Bowman’s capsule.
items.answer: Blood entering the glomerulus (a tight knot of capillaries) is under high pressure, forcing water, glucose, salts, urea and other small molecules out of the blood and into the surrounding Bowman’s capsule, forming the filtrate. Larger components of the blood, such as blood cells and large proteins, are too big to pass through the capillary walls and remain in the blood.
items.explanation: This filtration is described as "non-selective" at this stage — everything small enough to pass through is filtered out, regardless of whether the body actually needs it, which is why a subsequent selective reabsorption step is needed to recover useful substances from the filtrate.

items.prompt: Describe the process of selective reabsorption that occurs in the proximal convoluted tubule of the nephron.
items.answer: As the filtrate passes along the proximal convoluted tubule, useful substances that the body needs — such as all of the glucose, most of the water, and various salts — are actively reabsorbed back into the surrounding blood capillaries, while waste substances (such as urea) are largely left behind in the filtrate to continue toward the bladder as urine.
items.explanation: This process is described as "selective" because only useful substances are reabsorbed, in contrast to the non-selective filtration that occurred earlier at the glomerulus — this selectivity is essential for conserving valuable substances (glucose, water, salts) that would otherwise be wastefully lost in urine.

items.prompt: Explain the general role of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in regulating the water content of urine.
items.answer: ADH, released from the pituitary gland in response to a low blood water content (or high blood concentration), acts on the kidney tubules to increase the amount of water reabsorbed back into the blood from the filtrate, producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine. When blood water content is high, less ADH is released, so less water is reabsorbed, producing a larger volume of more dilute urine.
items.explanation: This hormonal control allows the kidney to continuously adjust the concentration and volume of urine produced according to the body’s current water balance, helping maintain a stable internal water content despite varying fluid intake and loss.

items.context: A drug used to treat high blood pressure works by blocking the transport proteins that pump salt out of the ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Patients taking it produce a much larger volume of urine than usual.
items.prompt: Explain how the loop of Henle normally allows concentrated urine to be produced, and use that mechanism to explain why blocking this one pump increases urine volume so much.
items.answer: The ascending limb actively pumps salt out of the filtrate into the surrounding medulla tissue. Because the loop doubles back on itself, that salt accumulates and the medulla becomes progressively saltier towards its deepest point, building a standing gradient. The collecting duct then carries the filtrate back down through this salty tissue, and at every level the tissue outside is saltier than the filtrate inside, so water leaves the filtrate by osmosis and is returned to the blood. The urine that emerges is therefore small in volume and concentrated, and the salt gradient is what makes that possible. Blocking the pump removes the first step and therefore everything that depends on it. With no salt pumped out, the medulla does not become salty and the gradient is never established. When the filtrate then passes down the collecting duct there is no osmotic gradient to draw water out of it, so the water stays in the filtrate and is lost as urine. The volume rises sharply. The effect is large out of proportion to the single pump blocked because that pump is not one of several water-saving mechanisms but the origin of the only gradient the kidney has for recovering water at this stage.
items.explanation: Follow the causal chain in order — pump salt, build gradient, draw water out — because the drug breaks the first link and the question is really about what the later links depended on. The lesson generalises: the kidney never moves water directly, it moves solutes and lets water follow, so anything that disturbs a solute gradient shows up immediately as a change in urine volume.

items.context: A learner tests their own urine with a glucose dipstick, finds no glucose, and concludes they cannot have diabetes. A nurse says the test is not sufficient to rule it out.
items.prompt: Whose position is better supported? Justify your answer by explaining why glucose is absent from healthy urine and present in untreated diabetes.
items.answer: The nurse's. In a healthy person, glucose is small enough to pass freely into the filtrate at the glomerulus, so it is all filtered out of the blood -- and then all of it is reabsorbed back into the blood along the proximal convoluted tubule by active transport. Because that reabsorption uses carrier proteins, it has a maximum rate: it can keep up with any amount of glucose a healthy blood concentration delivers, so none is left to appear in the urine. In untreated diabetes the blood glucose concentration is high, more glucose is filtered than the carriers can return, the excess remains in the tubule and is excreted -- and because it raises the solute concentration of the filtrate, it draws water with it osmotically, which is why untreated diabetics pass large volumes and are thirsty. The reason the learner's test proves nothing is that glucose only appears once the blood concentration exceeds that reabsorption threshold, which is well above the level at which diabetes is diagnosed. A person can have diabetes, and be doing damage, at blood concentrations that never spill into the urine -- and the reading also depends on when they last ate. Diabetes is diagnosed on blood glucose, not urine glucose, which is what the nurse is saying.
items.explanation: The test result is real and the threshold is what it hides. Level 4 is recognising that a negative on an insensitive test is not a negative.

items.prompt: Describe the function of the ureter, the bladder, and the urethra in the urinary system.
items.answer: The ureter is a muscular tube that carries urine from each kidney down to the bladder, using peristaltic (wave-like) contractions. The bladder is a muscular, expandable sac that stores urine until it is convenient to be released. The urethra is the tube through which urine is finally expelled from the bladder to the outside of the body.
items.explanation: Together, these three structures form the transport and temporary storage pathway for urine after it has been produced by the kidneys, allowing urine to be released under voluntary control (via the bladder) rather than continuously as it is produced.

items.prompt: The hormone that stimulates the development of male secondary sexual characteristics is …
items.answer: testosterone.
items.explanation: Testosterone is secreted by the testes from puberty.

items.prompt: The part of the ear that converts vibrations into nerve impulses is the …
items.answer: organ of Corti.
items.explanation: The organ of Corti, in the cochlea, contains the hair cells that are receptors for sound.

items.prompt: TSH, which stimulates the thyroid gland, is secreted by the …
items.answer: pituitary gland.
items.explanation: TSH is thyroid-stimulating hormone.

items.prompt: Which ONE of the following animals shows external fertilisation?
items.answer: Frog
items.explanation: Frogs release eggs and sperm into water.

items.prompt: When a person walks from a dark room into bright sunlight, the …

options.label: radial muscles of the iris contract and the pupil dilates.
circular muscles of the iris contract and the pupil constricts.
ciliary muscles relax and the pupil constricts.
suspensory ligaments tighten and the pupil dilates.

items.answer: circular muscles of the iris contract and the pupil constricts.
items.explanation: A smaller pupil lets less light into the eye and protects the retina.

items.prompt: If fertilisation does not take place, the corpus luteum breaks down and …

options.label: the oestrogen level rises and ovulation follows.
the progesterone level falls and menstruation begins.
the FSH level falls and a new follicle grows.
the LH level rises and implantation takes place.

items.answer: the progesterone level falls and menstruation begins.
items.explanation: Progesterone keeps the endometrium thick; without it the endometrium is shed.

items.prompt: Which ONE of the following happens when the body becomes too hot?

options.label: Vasoconstriction of the skin arterioles and less sweating
Vasodilation of the skin arterioles and more sweating
Vasodilation of the skin arterioles and less sweating
Vasoconstriction of the skin arterioles and more sweating

items.answer: Vasodilation of the skin arterioles and more sweating
items.explanation: More blood near the skin and more sweat both increase heat loss.

items.prompt: A stem bends towards light because auxin …

options.label: moves to the lit side and stimulates growth there.
