| Northern Europe | 90 |
| East African herders | 60 |
| East Asia | 10 |
(The figures are approximate.)
questions.prompt: Use the data and the passage to explain the differences between the three populations.
questions.answer: The ability is most common in Northern Europe (90%) and among East African herders (60%), groups with a long history of keeping cattle and drinking milk, where the mutation gave an advantage. It is rare in East Asia (10%), where milk was traditionally not part of the adult diet, so there was no selection for it.
questions.explanation: The pattern matches the history of dairy farming.

questions.context:
Rock pocket mice live in the desert. Most of the desert is covered with pale sand, but in some areas there are dark lava rocks. Owls hunt the mice from above.
|+ TABLE 4: DARK-FURRED MICE
| Habitat | Dark mice (%) |
|---|---|
| Dark lava rock | 95 |
| Pale sand | 5 |
(The figures are approximate.)
questions.prompt: Describe how natural selection could lead to most mice on the dark lava rock being dark.
questions.answer: There is variation in fur colour among the mice. On dark rock, pale mice are easily seen by owls and eaten, while dark mice are camouflaged. More dark mice survive and reproduce. They pass the allele for dark fur to their offspring. Over many generations, the proportion of dark mice on the lava increases.
questions.explanation: Marks: variation, predation of pale mice, survival of dark mice, inheritance, change over generations.

questions.prompt: Each turn of the Calvin cycle fixes one molecule of carbon dioxide, and glucose has six carbon atoms. How many turns of the cycle are needed to make 5 molecules of glucose? Show your working.
questions.answer: One glucose needs 6 carbon atoms, so 6 turns. 5 glucose molecules need 5 × 6 = 30 turns.
questions.explanation: Every carbon atom in the glucose comes from a carbon dioxide molecule fixed in the light-independent reactions.

questions.prompt: Name THREE substances the Calvin cycle needs in order to run.
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide, ATP and NADPH (hydrogen carried by NADP), all from the light phase except the carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: The light-independent reactions fix carbon dioxide and reduce it, using energy from ATP and hydrogen from NADPH.

questions.prompt: Describe what happens to carbon dioxide during the Calvin cycle.
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide combines with a five-carbon compound (RuBP) — carbon fixation. The product is reduced, using hydrogen from NADPH and energy from ATP, to form a three-carbon sugar (PGAL/G3P). Some of this sugar is used to build glucose; the rest regenerates RuBP so the cycle can continue.
questions.explanation: The cycle is called light-independent because it does not use light directly, but it stops in the dark once the ATP and NADPH from the light phase run out.

memo.text: Some makes glucose; the rest regenerates RuBP

questions.prompt: Amylase took 6 minutes to digest all the starch in a test tube at 37 °C, and 15 minutes at 20 °C. Calculate how many times faster the amylase worked at 37 °C, and explain the difference.
questions.answer: 15 ÷ 6 = 2,5 times faster. 37 °C is close to the optimum temperature for human amylase. At 20 °C the enzyme and starch molecules move more slowly and collide less often, so fewer starch molecules are broken down to maltose each minute.
questions.explanation: The shorter the time, the faster the rate: rate is proportional to 1 ÷ time, so the ratio of the times gives the ratio of the rates.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme breaks maltose down into glucose?
questions.answer: Maltase
questions.explanation: Amylase turns starch into maltose; maltase finishes the job by turning maltose into glucose.

questions.prompt: State the substrate of lipase, the products it forms, and where in the alimentary canal it acts.
questions.answer: Lipase acts on lipids (fats and oils) and breaks them down into fatty acids and glycerol. It acts in the small intestine (duodenum).
questions.explanation: Bile emulsifies the fats first, giving lipase a much larger surface to work on.

questions.prompt: Cellular respiration of one glucose molecule, using oxygen, releases about 38 ATP. A working muscle cell uses 1 900 000 ATP per second. Calculate how many glucose molecules it must respire each second, and state what the ATP is used for.
questions.answer: 1 900 000 ÷ 38 = 50 000 glucose molecules per second. The ATP supplies the energy for muscle contraction.
questions.explanation: ATP is the cell’s energy currency: respiration makes it, and work such as contraction, active transport and building molecules spends it.

questions.prompt: Calculate the total carbon dioxide the germinating seeds release in the time shown, explain why the boiled seeds were included, and state the conclusion about respiration.
questions.context:
Carbon dioxide released, measured for 6 hours at 25 °C:
Germinating seeds: 0,4 cm³ per hour
Boiled seeds (same mass): 0 cm³ per hour
questions.answer: 0,4 × 6 = 2,4 cm³. The boiled seeds are the control: boiling kills them, so they show that the carbon dioxide comes from living seeds and not from something else in the apparatus. Conclusion: living (germinating) seeds carry out cellular respiration and release carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: A control is identical except for the one factor being tested, here whether the seeds are alive.

memo.text: Boiled seeds are the control / dead seeds
Show the carbon dioxide comes from living seeds
Germinating seeds respire and release carbon dioxide

questions.prompt: What is meant by cellular respiration?

options.label: The movement of air into and out of the lungs
The controlled release of energy from glucose in living cells
The making of glucose using light energy
The exchange of gases across the alveoli

questions.answer: The controlled release of energy from glucose in living cells
questions.explanation: Option A is breathing, C is photosynthesis and D is gaseous exchange.

questions.context: At high altitude, the atmospheric partial pressure of oxygen is significantly lower than at sea level, even though oxygen still makes up 21% of the air.
questions.prompt: Explain why a person moving from sea level to a high-altitude environment initially experiences shortness of breath, and describe ONE way the body can adapt to this over several weeks.
questions.answer: At high altitude, air pressure is lower, so although oxygen still makes up 21% of the air, its actual partial pressure (concentration) available to diffuse into the blood at the alveoli is much lower than at sea level, reducing the concentration gradient driving oxygen diffusion from air into blood. Less oxygen therefore diffuses into the blood per breath, causing the person to breathe faster and more deeply — and feel short of breath — as the body attempts to take in enough oxygen. Over several weeks, the body can adapt by producing more red blood cells, increasing the blood’s haemoglobin concentration and hence its overall oxygen-carrying capacity, compensating for the reduced oxygen gradient at the alveoli.
questions.explanation: This shows that the rate of diffusion depends on the size of a concentration (partial pressure) gradient, not merely percentage composition, and illustrates a genuine long-term physiological adaptation (acclimatisation) to chronic low oxygen availability, rather than just a temporary behavioural response.

questions.context: A tobacco advertisement notes that most smokers never develop lung cancer, and that some non-smokers do, and concludes that the link between smoking and lung cancer is therefore unproven.
questions.prompt: Evaluate this argument. Justify your answer by explaining how tar in cigarette smoke contributes to lung cancer.
questions.answer: Both facts are true and the conclusion does not follow, because the argument demands a certainty that no cause of cancer has. Tar condenses onto the lining of the airways and contains carcinogens, chemicals that damage the DNA of the cells they are in prolonged contact with. Cancer arises when a cell accumulates enough mutations in the genes controlling cell division that it divides uncontrollably, and mutation is a chance event: a carcinogen raises the probability that a given cell is damaged in a given way, it does not determine it. Tar also paralyses and destroys the cilia, so the mucus that would normally sweep trapped material out stays put, which keeps the carcinogens in contact with the lining for far longer and raises the exposure further. So the mechanism predicts exactly what the advertisement reports: a higher risk in smokers, not a certainty, and a non-zero risk in non-smokers, who are exposed to other carcinogens and to chance mutations anyway. The same logic would say seatbelts are unproven because most people in crashes without one survive. What settles the question is the size and consistency of the difference -- smokers are many times more likely to develop lung cancer, the risk rises with the number smoked and the years smoked, and falls after stopping, which is the pattern a cause produces and coincidence does not. The argument is not a scientific objection; it is a misunderstanding of what a risk factor claims.
questions.explanation: The item tests the difference between a deterministic and a probabilistic cause, which is the reasoning the advertisement exploits.

questions.context: A person is exposed to air containing an abnormally low concentration of oxygen, such as at very high altitude.
questions.prompt: Explain how this low-oxygen environment would affect the rate and depth of the person’s breathing, and describe ONE long-term physiological adaptation the body could make if the person remained at high altitude for an extended period.
questions.answer: With a lower concentration of oxygen in the inhaled air, the concentration gradient driving oxygen diffusion from the alveoli into the blood is reduced, so less oxygen than usual is able to diffuse into the blood with each breath. This drop is detected (indirectly, via changes in blood chemistry) by receptors that stimulate the breathing control centre in the brain, causing the person to breathe both faster and more deeply in an attempt to take in more air (and hence more oxygen molecules) per unit time, partly compensating for the lower oxygen concentration. Over an extended period at high altitude, the body can adapt by increasing its production of red blood cells (and haemoglobin), increasing the blood’s overall oxygen-carrying capacity.
questions.explanation: This increased red blood cell production (a process called acclimatisation) is why endurance athletes sometimes train at high altitude for extended periods before competing at lower altitudes, where their temporarily increased oxygen-carrying capacity can improve performance.

questions.prompt: Name the excretory organ that removes each of the following from the body: (a) carbon dioxide, (b) nitrogenous waste in urine, (c) water and salts in sweat.
questions.answer: (a) Lungs. (b) Kidneys. (c) Skin.
questions.explanation: Excretion is the removal of waste made by the body’s own metabolism, and four organs share the work: the lungs breathe out carbon dioxide and some water vapour, the kidneys make urine that carries urea, excess water and salts, the skin loses water, salts and a little urea in sweat, and the liver makes the urea in the first place.

questions.prompt: Explain why the liver is counted as an excretory organ even though no waste leaves the body through the liver itself.
questions.answer: Excess amino acids cannot be stored. In the liver the amino group is removed from each excess amino acid (deamination) and converted to urea. The urea is released into the blood and carried to the kidneys, which excrete it in urine. The liver therefore makes the waste product that the kidneys remove.
questions.explanation: Excretion includes making a waste product safe to remove, not only removing it. Ammonia from the amino groups is toxic, so the liver converts it to urea, which is far less toxic and can travel in the blood to the kidneys.

memo.text: Excess amino acids cannot be stored
Deamination: the amino group is removed in the liver
Urea is carried in the blood to the kidneys and excreted in urine

questions.prompt: A learner says the lungs belong only to the breathing system and are not excretory organs. Explain why the lungs are also excretory organs.
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide (and some water vapour) is a waste product of cellular respiration in the body’s cells. The lungs remove this carbon dioxide from the body when we breathe out, so they excrete a metabolic waste.
questions.explanation: An organ is excretory if it removes a waste product of the body’s metabolism. Carbon dioxide is made by respiration inside cells, so removing it is excretion, even though the lungs are also used for gaseous exchange.

memo.text: Carbon dioxide is a waste product of cellular respiration
The lungs remove it from the body when exhaling

questions.prompt: Give TWO ways micro-organisms are beneficial in making food, and TWO ways they are beneficial in the environment.
questions.answer: Food: yeast in baking bread and brewing; bacteria in making yoghurt and cheese. Environment: decomposition of dead matter, which recycles nutrients; nitrogen fixation by bacteria, which adds nitrogen to the soil.
questions.explanation: Antibiotic production is also accepted as a useful role, but it is neither food nor environment.

questions.prompt: A doctor refuses to prescribe antibiotics to a patient with influenza. Explain why.
questions.answer: Influenza is caused by a virus. Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses, so they would not cure the illness (and unnecessary use helps bacteria become resistant).
questions.explanation: Viruses have no cell wall or bacterial machinery for the antibiotic to attack.

memo.text: Influenza is caused by a virus
Antibiotics have no effect on viruses

questions.prompt: Micro-organisms can be harmful. Name THREE human diseases, each caused by a different kind of micro-organism, and name the kind of micro-organism that causes each.
questions.answer: Bacterium: tuberculosis (or cholera). Virus: HIV/AIDS (or influenza, measles). Fungus: ringworm (or athlete’s foot, thrush).
questions.explanation: Knowing the cause decides the treatment: antibiotics for bacteria, antivirals for some viruses, antifungals for fungi.

questions.prompt: Name TWO ways in which seeds are important to humans.
questions.answer: Any two of: as staple food (maize, wheat, rice, beans); as a source of cooking oil (sunflower); as animal feed; as a source of income for farmers and traders; for growing the next season's crops.
questions.explanation: Most of the world's calories come from the seeds of a few grasses — maize, wheat and rice.

questions.prompt: Explain what a seed bank is, and give TWO reasons why seed banks are important for conserving plant diversity.
questions.answer: A seed bank stores seeds of many plant species, and varieties of crops, under controlled conditions. It protects species that are endangered in the wild from extinction, and keeps crop varieties that could be needed later — for example ones resistant to disease or drought — or that could be lost in a disaster.
questions.explanation: A seed bank is insurance: if a species or variety disappears from the field, it can be grown again from stored seed.

memo.text: Stores seeds of many species under controlled conditions
Keeps useful crop varieties for the future

questions.prompt: Seeds in a seed bank are dried until they hold very little water and are then kept at about −20 °C. Explain why these conditions keep the seeds alive for many years.
questions.answer: With very little water the seed cannot take up water to germinate, and its enzymes are inactive. The low temperature slows cellular respiration further, so the food store is used up extremely slowly. Dry, cold conditions also stop fungi and bacteria from growing on the seeds.
questions.explanation: Germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Removing the water and the warmth keeps the embryo alive but inactive.

memo.text: No water, so no germination and inactive enzymes
Low temperature slows respiration, saving the food store

questions.prompt: Using a pigeon as the example, explain how THREE structural features adapt an animal for flight.
questions.answer: Hollow bones make the skeleton light, so less energy is needed to stay in the air. Feathers provide a large, light surface for lift and streamlining. A keeled sternum gives a large area for attaching the powerful flight muscles. (Also accepted: forelimbs modified as wings that push against the air.)
questions.explanation: Each mark pair is a feature and what it does for flight; naming a feature without saying how it helps earns only half.

memo.text: give a large surface for lift
for attachment of large flight muscles

questions.prompt: Many animals have an exoskeleton. Explain TWO disadvantages of an exoskeleton for an animal’s size and lifestyle.
questions.answer: An exoskeleton becomes too heavy to support and move if the animal is large, so it limits the animal’s size. It cannot grow, so the animal must moult to grow; while the new exoskeleton hardens after moulting, the animal is soft and vulnerable to predators.
questions.explanation: Both disadvantages come from the skeleton being a rigid outer case rather than living bone inside the body.

memo.text: a large exoskeleton would be too heavy
vulnerable to predators until the new exoskeleton hardens

questions.prompt: A jellyfish’s body parts are arranged evenly around a central point, and it drifts with the currents. Explain how this body plan suits its lifestyle.
questions.answer: With radial symmetry the body is the same all round, so a drifting animal can detect and catch food, or meet danger, coming from any direction equally well.
questions.explanation: An animal that does not move in one direction has no "front"; radial symmetry lets it respond equally on every side.

memo.text: Body parts arranged equally around a centre
Can meet food or danger from any direction

questions.prompt: To estimate a population of lizards using mark-recapture, 60 lizards were caught, marked and released. A week later 50 were caught, of which 12 were marked. Estimate the population size.
questions.answer: Population = (first catch × second catch) ÷ number recaptured = (60 × 50) ÷ 12 = 250 lizards.
questions.explanation: The fraction marked in the second catch is taken to equal the fraction marked in the whole population.

questions.prompt: Five 1 m² quadrats were placed at random in a 200 m² field, and the aloe plants in each were counted: 4, 7, 3, 6, 5. Estimate the number of aloes in the field, and give ONE way to make the estimate more reliable.
questions.answer: Mean per quadrat = (4 + 7 + 3 + 6 + 5) ÷ 5 = 5 per m². Estimate = 5 × 200 = 1 000 aloes. Use more quadrats (or place them randomly over the whole field) so the sample better represents the field.
questions.explanation: Sampling assumes the quadrats are typical of the whole area, which is more likely the more of them there are.

questions.prompt: Oxpeckers eat ticks off a buffalo’s skin: the birds get food and the buffalo is rid of parasites. Which type of symbiosis is this?
questions.answer: Mutualism
questions.explanation: Both species benefit, which is mutualism. In commensalism only one benefits and the other is unaffected.

questions.context: A timber company clears 500 hectares of indigenous forest and plants 500 hectares of a single fast-growing exotic tree species, stating that the area under trees is unchanged and biodiversity is therefore preserved.
questions.prompt: Assess the company's statement. Justify your answer by referring to how deforestation causes a loss of biodiversity.
questions.answer: The statement is true about the area and false about the biodiversity, because a plantation is not a forest. An indigenous forest is structurally complex -- a canopy, an understorey, shrubs, ground layer, deadwood and leaf litter -- and it contains many tree species of different ages. That variety of layers and species is what provides the range of niches on which its animals, insects, fungi and smaller plants depend, and many of those species are specialists that live nowhere else. Clearing it destroys their habitat outright, and species with nowhere else to go are lost from the area entirely. A single-species plantation of even-aged trees offers one layer, one food plant and little ground cover; it is usually harvested before it develops complexity, and an exotic species supports few indigenous insects, which have not evolved to feed on it. So the replacement supports a small number of generalist species where the forest supported many specialised ones. There are further losses the area figure conceals: the forest's seed dispersers and pollinators disappear with it, so the surrounding forest regenerates less well; the soil and the leaf-litter community are destroyed by clearing; and if the cleared block connected two remaining forest patches, its loss fragments them. Equal area is not equal habitat, and the statement measures what is easy to count rather than what was lost.
questions.explanation: The arithmetic in the claim is correct. The marks are for identifying that structural and species complexity, not area, is what supports biodiversity.

questions.context: Catches of one fish species, in thousands of tonnes: 1970, 120. 1980, 310. 1988, 480. 1992, 190. 1996, 40. A fishing ban was imposed in 1997. By 2020, over twenty years later, catches after limited reopening were about 60. Fishing gear improved steadily throughout, and the fish reach breeding age at six years.
questions.prompt: Explain what the rise and fall in catches shows about the stock, and explain why the population had not returned to its former level more than twenty years after fishing stopped.
questions.answer: Rising catches to 1988 do not show a growing stock. Fishing gear was improving throughout, so more fish were being caught per unit of effort from a stock that was already being depleted — the catch figure measures fishing power as much as fish abundance, which is why a peak in catches often marks a stock already in trouble. The collapse after 1988 shows that the fish were being removed faster than they could reproduce: once the adults were largely gone, no amount of effort could find them, and the catch fell to almost nothing by 1996. The failure to recover has several causes working together. The fish breed at six years, so even an untouched population rebuilds slowly, and rebuilding cannot begin until enough survivors reach breeding age. Fishing had removed the large mature adults in particular, which are the most productive breeders, so the remaining stock reproduced poorly. Below a certain density, individuals may also struggle to find mates and the population can no longer grow effectively. Meanwhile other species had expanded into the space left behind and now compete with the young fish or eat them, so the ecosystem itself has shifted and no longer favours the original species returning to its former abundance.
questions.explanation: The most valuable point is that CATCH IS NOT ABUNDANCE — improving gear makes rising catches consistent with a shrinking stock, which is precisely how such collapses go unnoticed until they happen. The slow recovery needs more than one reason, and the strongest answers include the ecological one: the space a species vacates does not stay empty, so the system it must return to is no longer the system it left.

questions.context: A stretch of riverbank is dominated by an invasive alien tree. A landowner proposes to clear it with herbicide and leave the bank bare, arguing that once the invader is gone the indigenous plants will return on their own.
questions.prompt: Evaluate the landowner's proposal. Justify your answer by referring to how an invasive alien plant threatens indigenous plants.
questions.answer: Clearing is right and leaving the bank bare is likely to undo it. An invasive alien plant displaces indigenous plants by out-competing them for the resources both need: it typically grows faster and taller, shading them out; it takes a larger share of soil water and nutrients, often being deeper-rooted; and it occupies the space where indigenous seedlings would establish. Some also alter the habitat in ways that favour themselves -- changing soil chemistry, adding nitrogen to soils adapted to poor conditions, or changing how fire behaves -- and some release substances that suppress the germination of other species. The result is a dense stand where a varied indigenous community was, and with the plants go the insects, birds and other animals that depended on them. So removing it is necessary. The flaw is in what happens next. The invader leaves behind a large, long-lived seed bank in the soil, and bare cleared ground is exactly the condition its seedlings exploit best -- full light, no competition -- so it typically returns faster and denser than the indigenous species, whose seed sources may be far away and whose seedlings establish slowly. On a riverbank there is a second problem: bare soil with no root network erodes into the river, and the next flood takes it. The proposal should be extended to follow-up clearing of the regrowth for several seasons, and to replanting indigenous species immediately so that the ground is occupied and the bank is held.
questions.explanation: The diagnosis and the first step are both correct, so the learner cannot answer by rejecting the plan. The judgement is about what the cleared ground does next.

questions.prompt: State the positive result of each food test: (a) iodine solution for starch; (b) Benedict’s solution, heated, for reducing sugar; (c) Biuret reagent for protein; (d) the grease-spot test for lipids.
questions.answer: (a) Blue-black. (b) Brick-red (orange) precipitate. (c) Violet / purple. (d) A translucent spot on the paper.
questions.explanation: Benedict’s must be heated; the other three tests work at room temperature.

questions.prompt: A learner tests an unknown food solution. Iodine solution stays yellow-brown, Benedict’s solution stays blue after heating, and Biuret reagent turns violet. Deduce which organic compound the food contains and which it does not, giving the evidence for each.
questions.answer: It contains protein, because Biuret turned violet. It contains no starch, because iodine stayed yellow-brown, and no reducing sugar, because Benedict’s stayed blue.
questions.explanation: A negative test result is evidence too: the reagent keeps its own colour when the compound is absent.

memo.text: No reducing sugar -- Benedict’s stayed blue

questions.prompt: Two unlabelled beakers hold colourless solutions: one is glucose and one is starch. Describe a food test that would tell them apart, and the result you would expect for each solution.
questions.answer: Add a few drops of iodine solution to a sample of each. The starch solution turns blue-black; the glucose solution stays yellow-brown. (Also accepted: heat each with Benedict’s solution -- glucose gives a brick-red precipitate, starch stays blue.)
questions.explanation: Either test works because each reagent detects only one of the two carbohydrates; the other keeps the reagent’s own colour.

memo.text: Added to a sample of each solution

questions.context: A learner cuts six equal cylinders from the same potato, blots them dry, weighs each one, and leaves one in each of six sucrose solutions of different concentration for 30 minutes. She then blots and reweighs them, and records the percentage change in mass.
questions.prompt: Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable, and TWO variables she must keep constant. For each controlled variable, state what would go wrong if it were not controlled.
questions.answer: The independent variable is the concentration of the sucrose solution — it is what she deliberately changes. The dependent variable is the percentage change in mass of the potato cylinder — it is what she measures in response. Controlled variables, with the consequence of not controlling each: (1) TIME IN THE SOLUTION. If one cylinder sits for 45 minutes and another for 15, the longer one has more time for net water movement, so a difference in mass would show the effect of time rather than of concentration. (2) TEMPERATURE. Osmosis is faster when warmer, so cylinders at different temperatures would move water at different rates for reasons unrelated to the solution. (Either of these is also acceptable: the SIZE of the cylinders, since a larger surface area gives faster exchange and a heavier starting mass changes what a percentage means; or using the SAME potato, since different potatoes start with different internal solute concentrations.)
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one the investigator chooses, the dependent variable is the one that responds, and everything else that could plausibly affect the result must be held constant. Saying WHY each control matters is the part that earns marks — "keep the temperature the same" without a reason shows the rule was memorised rather than understood. Note why she measures PERCENTAGE change rather than change in grams: cylinders never start at exactly the same mass, and a percentage makes them comparable.

memo.text: Dependent variable: percentage change in mass
A correct consequence given for EACH controlled variable

questions.context: A microbiologist compares a cell of the bacterium Escherichia coli with a cell taken from human liver tissue.
questions.prompt: State which of the two cells is prokaryotic, and tabulate THREE structural differences between the E. coli cell and the human liver cell.
questions.answer: The E. coli cell is prokaryotic. E. coli has no true nucleus and its circular DNA lies free in the cytoplasm, while the liver cell has a nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane; E. coli has no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, while the liver cell has them; and E. coli has a cell wall containing peptidoglycan, while the human liver cell has no cell wall.
questions.explanation: The presence of a nuclear membrane and of membrane-bound organelles is the defining difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, and tabulating requires the same feature to be compared in each column.

questions.context: Cylinders of equal mass were cut from the same potato and left for one hour in three solutions. Change in mass: distilled water = +8%; 0,5 mol·dm⁻³ sucrose = −2%; 1,0 mol·dm⁻³ sucrose = −11%.
questions.prompt: Explain the change in mass of the cylinders in the distilled water and in the 1,0 mol·dm⁻³ sucrose solution in terms of water movement.
questions.answer: In distilled water the water potential outside the cylinder was higher than inside the potato cells, so water moved by osmosis through the selectively permeable cell membranes into the cells, the cells became turgid and the mass increased by 8%. The 1,0 mol·dm⁻³ sucrose was more concentrated and had a lower water potential than the cell sap, so water moved by osmosis out of the cells, the cells became flaccid or plasmolysed and the mass decreased by 11%.
questions.explanation: Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a high to a low water potential across a selectively permeable membrane, so the direction of that movement decides whether the tissue gains or loses mass.

questions.prompt: Describe how cytokinesis takes place in an animal cell and in a plant cell, and explain why the two are different.
questions.answer: In an animal cell the cell membrane pinches inwards (furrows) until the cytoplasm divides into two cells. In a plant cell a cell plate forms between the two nuclei and grows outwards to become the new cell wall. The difference is because the rigid cell wall of a plant cell cannot pinch in.
questions.explanation: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm after the nucleus has divided.

memo.text: Plant: cell plate forms between the nuclei
Cell plate becomes the new cell wall
Rigid cell wall cannot pinch in

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a benign tumour and a malignant tumour, and name the process by which cancer spreads.
questions.answer: A benign tumour stays in one place. A malignant tumour invades nearby tissue and spreads to other organs. The spreading is called metastasis.
questions.explanation: Only malignant tumours are cancers; benign tumours can still cause harm by pressing on organs.

questions.prompt: Chemotherapy drugs stop cells dividing by mitosis. Explain why chemotherapy shrinks a tumour, and why patients often lose their hair during treatment.
questions.answer: A tumour is a mass of cells dividing by uncontrolled mitosis, so stopping mitosis stops it growing and it shrinks. The drugs also act on normal cells that divide rapidly, such as hair-follicle cells, so hair stops growing and falls out.
questions.explanation: The drugs target dividing cells in general, not cancer cells only, which is why side effects appear in tissues that divide often.

memo.text: Tumour cells divide rapidly by uncontrolled mitosis
Hair-follicle cells also divide rapidly, so are affected

questions.context: A farmer rings a tree by removing a complete band of bark and phloem right round the trunk near the ground, intending to kill it. A neighbour says the tree will die within weeks because it can no longer take up water.
questions.prompt: Assess the neighbour's reasoning. Justify your answer, and predict what happens above and below the ring over the following months.
questions.answer: The neighbour is right that the tree will die and wrong about the mechanism, and the mechanism is what determines how long it takes. Removing the bark takes the phloem with it but leaves the xylem, which lies deeper in the trunk. Water and dissolved minerals are transported upwards in the xylem, so that pathway is intact and the leaves go on receiving water and go on photosynthesising -- the tree does not die of thirst in weeks. What is cut is the phloem, which carries the sugars made in the leaves downwards to the rest of the plant. Above the ring, sugars arriving from the leaves can go no further and accumulate, so the bark just above the cut often swells. Below the ring, the roots receive no sugars at all. They cannot photosynthesise, so they respire their stored reserves, and when those are exhausted the root cells die. Only then does water uptake fail, and the tree above dies afterwards -- which is why ringing kills over months to a season rather than in weeks, and why the top of the tree can look healthy for a surprisingly long time. So the neighbour's prediction is correct by accident: the tree does eventually die of water shortage, but as the final consequence of starving the roots rather than as the direct result of the cut.
questions.explanation: The conclusion is right and the reasoning wrong, which the item separates by asking for the sequence and the timescale rather than the outcome.

questions.context: Parenchyma occurs in the mesophyll of a leaf, in the cortex of a stem and in the flesh of a potato tuber.
questions.prompt: Explain how the same basic tissue can carry out photosynthesis in the leaf but storage in the potato tuber, referring to the features the cells share and to the ways in which they differ.
questions.answer: All parenchyma cells share the same basic plan, since they are living, thin-walled, roughly spherical cells with a large central vacuole and air spaces between them, and they stay unspecialised enough to take on different functions. In the leaf the parenchyma cells contain many chloroplasts, are arranged as a palisade layer close to the upper surface and are surrounded by intercellular air spaces that allow carbon dioxide to reach them, so they photosynthesise. In the potato tuber the cells are underground and receive no light, so they contain leucoplasts instead of chloroplasts and are packed with starch grains formed from sucrose delivered by the phloem, so they act as a storage tissue.
questions.explanation: Parenchyma is the least specialised plant tissue, so its function in a particular organ depends chiefly on which plastids are present and on where the tissue lies in the plant.

questions.context: Two transverse sections of a dicotyledonous plant are examined. In section A the vascular tissue lies in separate bundles arranged in a ring near the outside, with xylem towards the inside of each bundle and phloem towards the outside. In section B the vascular tissue lies as a single star-shaped core in the centre, with strips of phloem between the arms of the xylem.
questions.prompt: Identify the organ shown in section A and in section B, give a reason for each identification, and explain ONE advantage of the arrangement seen in each organ.
questions.answer: Section A is a stem, because the vascular tissue occurs as separate bundles arranged in a ring towards the outside with xylem and phloem in the same bundle. Section B is a root, because the vascular tissue forms a single central star-shaped cylinder with xylem and phloem in separate alternating strips. In the stem the peripheral ring of bundles, each containing thickened xylem and sclerenchyma, resists bending and keeps the stem upright so that the leaves are held out towards the light. In the root the central core of xylem resists the pulling forces exerted on the root when the shoot is tugged by wind, and its central position allows water absorbed across the cortex from all directions to be collected in one place.
questions.explanation: The distribution of strengthening tissue matches the mechanical stress on each organ, since bending forces on an aerial stem are best resisted by strength at the periphery while tension on a root is best resisted by strength in the centre.

questions.context: A Weddell seal hunting under the ice of Antarctic waters has a layer of blubber up to 8 cm thick beneath its skin.
questions.prompt: Name the type of connective tissue that makes up this layer, and explain FOUR ways in which the tissue benefits the seal.
questions.answer: The layer is adipose tissue. It insulates the seal by trapping heat and reducing heat loss to the freezing water; it stores fat as a long-term energy reserve for periods when the seal does not feed; it cushions and protects the underlying organs against knocks and pressure; and because fat is less dense than water it increases buoyancy, so the seal uses less energy to stay afloat between dives.
questions.explanation: Adipose tissue consists of cells swollen with stored lipid droplets in a loose fibrous matrix, and all four benefits follow directly from the physical properties of that stored lipid.

questions.context: A learner claims that smooth muscle must be weaker than skeletal muscle, since skeletal muscle can lift heavy weights while smooth muscle only moves food along a tube.
questions.prompt: Evaluate this claim. Justify your answer by referring to how smooth muscle brings about peristalsis and why it can work for long periods without tiring.
questions.answer: The claim compares the two on one measure and misses what each is built for. Smooth muscle in the oesophagus wall is arranged in two layers, circular and longitudinal, and they act antagonistically: behind the food the circular muscle contracts and the longitudinal relaxes, narrowing the tube and squeezing the food forward, while ahead of it the longitudinal contracts and the circular relaxes, shortening and widening the tube to receive it. That wave, repeated along the length, is peristalsis, and it moves food regardless of gravity -- which is why a person can swallow lying down or upside down. The muscle is unstriated and under involuntary control, so it operates without conscious effort, and it contracts slowly and sustains contraction with far less energy than skeletal muscle uses; it is well supplied with blood and respires aerobically, so lactic acid does not accumulate and it does not fatigue. Judged against its job, that is a demanding specification and skeletal muscle would fail at it: skeletal muscle contracts fast and powerfully and tires quickly, which suits lifting and running and would be useless for a task that must continue every hour of a lifetime without rest or attention. So "weaker" is measuring force over a short interval, and each muscle type is better than the other at what it does -- which is the point the learner has missed.
questions.explanation: The comparison is real and the criterion is too narrow. Level 4 is judging each tissue against the demands it actually meets.

questions.context: A young athlete damages the cartilage in a knee joint. They ask why it cannot simply be left to heal like the broken arm they had as a child, which mended completely in six weeks.
questions.prompt: Assess whether the comparison with the broken arm is a fair one. Justify your answer by referring to the structure of the cartilage on the ends of the bones.
questions.answer: The comparison is not fair, and the difference lies in the blood supply rather than in the severity of the injury. The cartilage on the ends of the bones in a joint is hyaline cartilage: a firm but slightly flexible tissue of chondrocytes embedded in a smooth, glassy matrix. That smooth surface, together with the synovial fluid, is what lets the bone ends slide over one another with very little friction, and the slight flexibility allows it to absorb shock as the joint is loaded. What it does not have is blood vessels -- it is avascular, and the chondrocytes are supplied only by substances diffusing slowly through the matrix from surrounding tissue. Bone is the opposite: it is richly supplied with blood, so after a fracture a clot forms, cells and nutrients are delivered to the site in quantity, and new bone tissue is built and remodelled, which is why the arm healed completely in weeks. Damaged cartilage receives no such delivery. Repair cells and nutrients cannot reach the site in useful numbers, so healing is extremely slow and usually incomplete, and what does form is a weaker fibrous tissue rather than proper hyaline cartilage. That is why cartilage damage tends to persist, to worsen with continued use, and to need surgical help rather than time. So the athlete's expectation is reasonable and rests on an assumption -- that all tissues repair like bone -- that this tissue does not meet.
questions.explanation: The comparison is one a learner would naturally make. The marks are for identifying the structural property that makes one tissue repair well and the other not.

questions.context: A leafy shoot was fitted into a bubble potometer. The distance the air bubble moved in 10 minutes was recorded: still air 24 mm; in front of a fan 61 mm; with a plastic bag over the leaves 5 mm.
questions.prompt: Explain the effect of the fan and the effect of the plastic bag on the distance moved by the bubble.
questions.answer: The fan moved the bubble much further, 61 mm, because the moving air blew away the layer of water vapour that collects around the leaf, keeping the water potential gradient between the leaf air spaces and the outside air steep, so transpiration and therefore water uptake increased. The plastic bag reduced the distance to 5 mm because water vapour was trapped inside the bag, the humidity around the leaves rose, the gradient became very shallow and little water vapour could diffuse out, so very little water was taken up.
questions.explanation: The bubble measures water uptake, which is almost equal to the rate of transpiration, so anything that changes the steepness of the water vapour gradient at the leaf surface changes the distance the bubble moves.

questions.context: A pot plant is not watered for four days. Its leaves and young stems droop, but after the pot is watered the plant is upright again within two hours.
questions.prompt: Explain, at cellular level, why the plant drooped and why watering restored it, and name the tissue that supplies most of the support in these young, soft stems.
questions.answer: As the soil dried out the cells lost more water by transpiration than they absorbed, so water left the vacuoles by osmosis, the vacuoles shrank and the cytoplasm and cell membrane no longer pressed outwards on the cell wall. The cells therefore lost their turgor pressure and became flaccid, and since the soft leaves and young stems depend on the outward push of turgid cells to keep them firm, the plant drooped. After watering, the soil water potential became higher than that of the root cells, so water was absorbed by osmosis, moved up the xylem and entered the cells, which swelled until the cell wall resisted further expansion and the cells became turgid again, restoring the firmness of the leaves and stems. Turgid parenchyma, assisted by living collenchyma in the stem, supplies most of the support in these young soft stems.
questions.explanation: Support in a soft herbaceous plant is hydraulic, so it depends on cell turgor and is therefore lost and regained within hours, unlike the permanent support given by lignified tissue in a woody stem.

questions.context: Two shrubs were compared. Species P grows in the Namaqualand desert and has small, thick leaves with a thick cuticle and stomata sunken in pits lined with hairs. Species Q grows beside a stream in KwaZulu-Natal and has large, thin leaves with a thin cuticle and stomata level with the surface. Water lost per 100 cm² of leaf in one hour: P = 0,6 g; Q = 4,1 g.
questions.prompt: Use the structural features given to explain the difference in the mass of water lost by the two species, and explain ONE disadvantage of the leaf structure of species P.
questions.answer: Species P lost far less water because its thick waxy cuticle waterproofs the leaf surface and blocks evaporation through the epidermis, its small leaves present a much smaller surface area for evaporation, and its sunken, hair-lined stomata trap a pocket of humid air just outside each pore so that the water potential gradient between the leaf and the air stays shallow and diffusion out of the leaf is slow. Species Q has a large surface area, a thin cuticle and exposed stomata from which water vapour is swept away easily, so it lost 4,1 g. The disadvantage for species P is that the same features that restrict water loss also restrict the entry of carbon dioxide and reduce the area available to absorb light, so its rate of photosynthesis and therefore its rate of growth are low.
questions.explanation: Xerophytic adaptations always involve a trade-off, because the leaf cannot be sealed against water loss without simultaneously restricting the gas exchange on which photosynthesis depends.

questions.prompt: When you bend your arm at the elbow, which muscle contracts and which muscle relaxes?
questions.answer: The biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes.
questions.explanation: To straighten the arm the opposite happens: the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes.

questions.prompt: Explain why skeletal muscles work in antagonistic pairs.
questions.answer: A muscle can only pull when it contracts; it cannot push. So a second muscle is needed to pull the bone back the other way. While one muscle of the pair contracts, the other relaxes.
questions.explanation: Biceps and triceps, and the hamstrings and quadriceps of the thigh, are examples of antagonistic pairs.

memo.text: Muscles can only pull/contract, not push
A second muscle pulls the bone back the opposite way
One contracts while the other relaxes

questions.prompt: A condition in which bones lose density and become brittle, so that they break easily, is called…
questions.answer: osteoporosis
questions.explanation: Osteoporosis is most common in older people, especially women after menopause.

questions.prompt: Blood flows at about 30 cm/s in the largest artery but only about 0,03 cm/s in the capillaries. Calculate how many times slower it flows in the capillaries, and explain why this slow flow is useful.
questions.answer: 30 ÷ 0,03 = 1 000 times slower. Slow flow gives more time for oxygen, glucose and wastes to diffuse between the blood and the tissue cells through the thin capillary walls.
questions.explanation: The capillaries together have a far larger cross-sectional area than the arteries feeding them, so the blood slows down there -- exactly where exchange with the tissues happens.

memo.text: of oxygen/nutrients/wastes by diffusion through the thin walls

questions.prompt: Which blood vessel has walls only one cell thick?
questions.answer: Capillary
questions.explanation: Capillary walls are a single layer of flat cells, so substances can diffuse through them easily.

questions.prompt: Tabulate TWO structural differences between the walls of arteries and veins.
questions.answer: Artery: thick, muscular, elastic wall; narrow lumen; no valves (except at the base of the aorta and pulmonary artery). Vein: thin wall with less muscle; wide lumen; valves along its length.
questions.explanation: A table needs headings for both vessels, with each difference compared in the same row. Two correct, matched rows earn the marks.

memo.text: Table with headings for artery and vein

questions.context:
DDT, a pesticide, was washed into a lake. The table shows its concentration in parts per million (ppm) at each level of the food chain.
|+ TABLE: DDT IN A LAKE FOOD CHAIN
| Level | DDT (ppm) |
|---|---|
| Water | 0,00005 |
| Plankton | 0,04 |
| Small fish | 0,5 |
| Large fish | 2 |
| Fish-eating birds | 25 |
questions.prompt: Calculate how many times more concentrated DDT is in the fish-eating birds than in the small fish, and explain why the pesticide has its greatest effect on the birds.
questions.answer: 25 ÷ 0,5 = 50 times. DDT is not broken down or excreted, so it is stored in the body. Each consumer eats many organisms from the level below and keeps the DDT from all of them, so the concentration increases at each trophic level.
questions.explanation: Bioaccumulation explains why top predators are harmed first by a pesticide that is found only in tiny amounts in the water.

questions.prompt: In a food web on a farm, jackals eat rabbits and rabbits eat grass. A farmer shoots all the jackals, so the predator is removed. Predict and explain the effect on the rabbits and on the grass.
questions.answer: With the predator removed, fewer rabbits are eaten, so the rabbit population increases. The larger rabbit population eats more grass, so the grass is over-grazed and decreases. Eventually the rabbits run short of food and their numbers may fall again.
questions.explanation: Removing one species changes every organism linked to it in the web, not only its direct prey.

questions.prompt: Explain why one species being removed from a food web can have an effect on the organisms that never feed on it directly.
questions.answer: Organisms in a food web are linked through many feeding relationships. A change in one population changes the populations that eat it and that it eats, and those changes pass on to the organisms linked to them in turn.
questions.explanation: The effect of a change spreads along every link in the web.

memo.text: Organisms are interlinked in the web
A change in one population passes on through the populations linked to it

questions.context: A large area of indigenous forest on a mountain slope is cleared for building.
questions.prompt: Explain how the removal of the trees affects the water cycle in that area, referring to at least THREE of its processes.
questions.answer: Transpiration falls sharply because the leaves that returned water vapour to the atmosphere have been removed, so less water vapour rises from the slope, less condensation takes place above it and local rainfall may decrease. Infiltration into the soil also decreases because there are no longer roots and leaf litter to hold the soil open and to slow the water down, so less water soaks in to recharge the groundwater. Consequently surface run-off increases, and rain now flows quickly down the bare slope, carrying topsoil with it, which causes erosion and flooding of the rivers below while leaving the slope drier between rains.
questions.explanation: Vegetation is a working part of the water cycle rather than a passive user of water, so removing it shifts water from the slow pathways of transpiration and infiltration to the fast pathway of run-off.

questions.context: A farmer applies large quantities of nitrate fertiliser to a field beside a dam. Within a few weeks the dam turns bright green, and a month later many dead fish are floating on the surface.
questions.prompt: Explain the sequence of events that links the fertiliser to the death of the fish, and name this process.
questions.answer: Rain washed the excess nitrates off the field into the dam, a process called leaching and run-off. The extra nitrates acted as nutrients for the algae and other water plants, which multiplied rapidly to form an algal bloom that turned the water green and covered the surface. The mat of algae blocked the light reaching the plants beneath, so those plants died, and when the short-lived algae died as well the dead material was broken down by enormous numbers of decomposing bacteria. These bacteria respired aerobically and used up most of the dissolved oxygen in the water, so the fish could not obtain enough oxygen for respiration and suffocated. The whole process is called eutrophication.
questions.explanation: Eutrophication shows how a nutrient that is beneficial on land becomes destructive in water, because the damage is done not by the nitrate itself but by the oxygen depletion that follows the boom and collapse of the algal population.

questions.context: A learner suggests that if all the fungi and bacteria in a forest could be destroyed, the trees would grow better because nothing would rot their fallen leaves.
questions.prompt: Evaluate this suggestion, explaining the role of decomposers in nutrient cycling and predicting what would actually happen to the forest.
questions.answer: The suggestion is wrong. Decomposers secrete enzymes onto dead leaves, dead animals and wastes and break the complex organic compounds in them down into simple inorganic substances such as ammonium compounds, nitrates, phosphates and carbon dioxide, which is the only route by which the nutrients locked up in dead bodies are returned to the soil and the air. Without them the leaf litter and dead wood would pile up on the forest floor, and all the carbon, nitrogen and mineral salts in that litter would stay locked inside the dead tissue. The trees would then be unable to absorb the mineral salts they need to build proteins and chlorophyll, growth would slow, the trees would show deficiency symptoms such as yellowing leaves, and the forest would eventually die because the nutrient cycles would have been broken.
questions.explanation: Decomposers are the link that closes every nutrient cycle, and recognising that nutrients are finite and must be recycled is what shows why removing them would starve the producers rather than protect them.
